chapter_theme: Civakan, seized at Kattiyangaran's order and bound at his parents' word, tells the grieving women of his house that one who knows births and release does not grieve; the city's women run from their games and crafts to lament, blaming karma, their own want of penance, the king and the father; Kantukkatan forbids the weeping, boasts the house's firmness, and as his son goes like a lion bound with a spider's thread, sends twelve crores of gold to cool the king's anger.

cast.role: the hero, raised by Kantukkatan, seized and bound at the usurper's order (புலவலன், பூணான் here)
the merchant's daughter whom Civakan saved from the elephant
the women of Civakan's household, likened to goddesses of the house
the women of the city's streets and houses
the people of Rajamapuram, the old city
the merchant who raised Civakan, his father here (தாதை, கந்துகன்)
Kantukkatan's wife, who raised Civakan (named in 1109)
the usurping minister now ruling, who has ordered Civakan seized (not named in this run)

1094.reading: Gunamalai, holding up her silk as the men lead Civakan away, cries twice that this is not fitting for her lord and is like a flower garland fallen into fire.
1094.event: Gunamalai cries out that the arrest is not fitting for her lord and wilts in grief.

1095.reading: The women of the mansion, like goddesses of the house, run out like peacocks fleeing a burning hill, learn what has happened and raise a cry of lament to the lion-shouldered one.
1095.event: The women of Civakan's house run out, learn of his arrest and lament aloud.

1096.reading: To these women, sinking in grief like a doe caught in a whirlpool of the Ganges, the learned hero speaks the words that follow.
1096.event: Civakan turns to the grieving women of his house to speak to them.
1096.nuance: The narrator names him புலவலன், the one skilled in learning, at the moment he is bound: the title prepares the doctrinal consolation of the next verse rather than any warrior's answer.

1097.reading: Civakan says that he, who has understood within how souls appear in the states of birth as one wakes from heavy sleep, how life leaves, and how it gains release and rises, will not melt in grief; attachment even the size of a split sesame seed is a fault, so they must not grieve.
1097.event: Civakan, bound and led away, forbids his household to grieve.

claims.claim: one who understands how souls are born into the states of existence, leave the body and rise in release does not grieve at misfortune
attachment, even as small as a split sesame seed, is a fault

1097.nuance: கதிகள் (the states of birth) and release as rising (வீடுபெற்று உயருமாறு) are the Jain frame the poem uses elsewhere; the school is the text's vocabulary, not a label added. The sesame measure (எட்பக அனைத்தும்) is the Kural's phrase for a small inner enmity (Kural 889, எட்பக வன்ன), but only two words match, so it is not marked as an echo.

1098.reading: As the women, having lost their jewel, fall to the ground wilting like young naga women robbed of their gem, Civakan in gem-bright ornaments passes gate after gate like the moon moving across the sky in the mouth of the eclipse planet.
1098.event: Civakan is led out through the many gates of the house while its women collapse.
1098.nuance: The eclipse image (மதியம் கோள்வாய்) makes the arrest a temporary swallowing: the moon in the planet's mouth still shines and will come out.

1099.reading: The young women of the city, crying that their hearts are burnt, leave their balls, dolls, play-stones and toy houses and run out with tinkling anklets to look.
1099.event: Young girls of the city drop their games and run out to see Civakan led away.

1100.reading: Women with jasmine garlands slipping and earrings flashing leave their vinas, breathe hot sighs and run till the street is full, anklets crying out.
1100.event: Women leave their vinas and crowd the street.

1101.reading: Women whose dark hair falls over their necks and whose breasts flush red throw down the balls that have made their palms ache, come there and are bewildered.
1101.event: Women at ball-play leave it and come, dazed with grief.

1102.reading: Garlanded women, their hearts melting, shed hot tears from kohl-lined eyes like the sea casting pearls and cry with great love, 'What can we do, O lord?'
1102.event: Women weep and cry out to Civakan in helpless love.

1103.reading: The dancing women, slender as lightning, run burning through the street with gold ear-rolls falling, jewels scattering and hair coming loose, asking what has befallen their beloved.
1103.event: The dancing women of the city run through the street asking what has happened to him.

1104.reading: Women with spear-long eyes brimming beat their bellies in grief, saying that if the garlanded one's beauty fades, the body will go and life itself will perish today.
1104.event: Women beat their bellies and say their lives will end if his beauty is harmed.
1104.nuance: நீயும் (line 2) addresses someone, perhaps a companion or the woman's own life; the line is read as a lament without fixing the addressee.

1105.reading: Young women throw off their honeyed garlands and ornaments and come to look, asking whether he who was like the wish-granting creeper of desire has come to this, their slender waists aching as they run.
1105.event: Women cast off their ornaments and run to look at him.

1106.reading: Some women restring the gems of girdles that broke, others scatter them as they run, and the flower-like women come before the garlanded one, crying that this is not fit, and beat their bellies.
1106.event: Women run before Civakan crying that his arrest is unjust and beat their bellies.
1106.nuance: Line 1 (மாதரார்கள் கற்பினுக்கு உடைந்த மாமணிக்கலை) is hard to construe: the girdles may have broken in the women's haste, or the line may say that their steadfastness gave way at the sight of him; the reading leaves it open.

1107.reading: Women who had been at their painting, with brush-box, board and fine colours, leave them, wilt like peacocks in distress, and with garlands scorched by their burning breath come and cling to the gateway.
1107.event: Women leave their painting and cling to the gate to see him.

1108.reading: Some women shake their hands and say 'see the fruit of deeds', some fear that if he is taken in this state the king will strike him, some say that his beauty, grace and learning will end today, and some say their hearts whirl like a potter's wheel.
1108.event: The city women speak their fears and griefs as Civakan is led away.

claims.claim: what befalls a man is the ripening of his deeds

1108.nuance: The karma explanation is one voice among several in a crowd; the next verse blames the father and the king in the same breath, so the poem gives the arrest more than one cause without settling which.

1109.reading: Some say the women did no penance to deserve him, some point to his hurt shoulders, some say the king has beckoned Death and will perish with his line, some that the father's act was a cruelty unfit to be done, some that Sunandai cannot bear it, and some cry out to dharma that it is not right.
1109.event: The city women blame their own lack of merit, the king and Civakan's father for the arrest.

claims.claim: those who have done no penance do not get to keep what they love
one who provokes the stronger calls Death down on himself and his line
a father who hands over his son to harm commits a cruelty

1109.nuance: Merit (நோற்றிலர்), the king's folly and the father's choice are all blamed here together, beside the previous verse's 'fruit of deeds'. The father's act was itself a decision to submit (verses 1089-1091), so the women condemn what the story has framed as prudence. கூற்றத்தைக் கொம்மை கொட்டி recalls Kural 894 (கூற்றத்தைக் கையால் விளித்தற்றால்) in sense, but only one word matches, so it is not marked as an echo.

1110.reading: Some say, 'weigh it: if this bull raged, would the king survive?'; some say he would guard the whole world as its ruler; some say it is great luck and this too is a turn of fate; some say 'do not stare, he is ashamed, the keen and courtly one.'
1110.event: The city women say Civakan could overpower the king and is fit to rule, and pity his shame.

claims.claim: this too is a portion allotted by fate

1110.nuance: The women's wish that he would guard the world as king is unknowing irony: he is the dead king's son, though no one here knows it. Line 3 (பாக்கயம் பெரிதுமே காண்) may mean the king's good fortune that Civakan does not resist, or the city's luck in such a man; the reading is not fixed.

1111.reading: Some say the sharp fingers that, removing the sulks of golden women, set right their anklets and grew red are now hurt; some say that if the lord all praise loses his beauty, let the old city of towers and mansions perish as food for Death.
1111.event: The city women lament his bound hands and curse the city if he is harmed.

1112.reading: Crying that this is unfit for the strong shoulders trained with the great bow that freed the herd seized by the black-bowed hunters, the old city behind its guarded walls is thrown into tumult like a dark sea churned by a mountain.
1112.event: The whole city rises in grief and uproar at the arrest.

1113.reading: As the crowds move thus, the father of the hero of the fire-hot arrows, seeing the great city's grief and the tears that laid the dust at their feet, tells them, as the spear-bearer who fights in war, not to weep.
1113.event: Kantukkatan sees the city's grief and tells the people not to weep.
1113.nuance: பொங்கமர் உழக்கும் வேலான் (line 4) gives the merchant a warrior's epithet; it may refer to the son rather than the father, which would change who forbids the weeping.

1114.reading: The speaker says that if one with lightning splits a mountain in two, it is the striker who shakes, not 'we', deeper than the mountain; such is the justice resolved, which even Yama cannot overturn; can anyone on the wide earth live standing against me?
1114.nuance: The speech is most likely Kantukkatan's, following his 'do not weep' in 1113, but the first person (துளங்கலம், என்னை) could be the house speaking, or Civakan's words reported; the defiant tone sits oddly with the father who just reasoned that opposing a king is the deed of the doomed (1089).

1115.reading: The speaker says the king has set out to snare a maned lion by netting the curved sea and fencing it with mountains; let him snare it if he can, but if he stands ready to cleave me with the sword while my kin weep, his own head, its garland scattered, will lie on the ground.
1115.nuance: The lion is Civakan, and the net of sea and mountains says the king's means are absurdly large and still too weak; who 'me' (என்னை) is, the father or the son, is not certain.

1116.reading: Civakan, like a long golden hill, whose sword burns in war among dark cloud-coloured elephants, walks on while the festive old city follows weeping, like a lion bound with a spider's thread.
1116.event: Civakan is led away bound while the city follows weeping.
1116.nuance: The spider's thread (சிலம்பி நூல்) makes the binding his own consent: the bond could not hold him, and what holds him is the word given to his parents (1091).

1117.reading: Kantukkatan, reckoning that a king's anger is a hot fire that will die down if gold rains on it like lightning-lit cloud, and otherwise will smoke, flare and burn all who come near, sends twelve crores of red gold and speaks humbly to the king.
1117.event: Kantukkatan sends twelve crores of gold to the king and pleads humbly for his son.

claims.claim: a king's anger is a fire that burns all near it unless quenched with gifts

1117.nuance: The merchant answers royal anger with money, the means of his own class, after the city's laments and his own defiant words; the plea itself begins in the next verse.

links.note: The Kural likens death to sleep and birth to waking; Civakan uses the waking from heavy sleep for the soul's appearing in the states of birth, adds release as a third motion, and draws from it a refusal to grieve at his own arrest.
links.teaches: The Kural's calm figure of sleep and waking only describes the cycle, while the Cintamani makes it an argument for conduct, so understanding birth as waking becomes the ground for refusing grief, and the cycle gains an exit the couplet never names.

gains.a: the hero's consolation is seen to rest on a figure the ethical tradition already held, which makes his calm learned rather than merely brave
gains.b: the couplet's image is shown as the first step of a larger scheme in which knowing the cycle aims at leaving it

links.note: Both measure a small but fatal thing as a split sesame seed: the Kural an inner enmity that holds ruin, Civakan the least attachment, which he calls a fault.
links.teaches: The sesame measure moves from a king's household enemy to the attachment inside the self, so the danger the Kural locates in a court the Jain hero locates in the heart that clings.

gains.a: Civakan's rule is given a familiar measure of how little it takes to ruin, transferred from politics to the soul
gains.b: the couplet's warning that a tiny hidden thing contains ruin is extended to attachment, a second enemy within

links.note: Saccandan, before his death, tells Vijayai that dying and being born come from one's deeds and that grief comes from want of understanding; his son, now seized by the same usurper, tells the women of his house that one who knows births and release will not grieve.
links.teaches: Father and son meet the usurper's violence with the same doctrinal consolation to the women who love them, but the father dies after speaking it and the son walks on alive, so the teaching recurs as the epic's own answer to tyranny rather than one man's farewell.

links.note: The city women see Civakan's arrest as the fruit of deeds; the dog beaten at the festival was said to have fallen into the net of strong karma, and Civakan freed it with the five mantras.
links.teaches: The same karmic explanation covers the beaten dog and the bound hero, but the story has already shown Civakan's own good deed to that dog, so the crowd's 'fruit of deeds' is about to ripen as the god's rescue of him.

links.note: The Kural says the weak who harm the strong beckon Death with their hand; the city women say the king who seizes Civakan has clapped his hands at Death and will perish with his line.
links.teaches: The women apply the couplet against the one who holds power, so the 'weak' party is the reigning king and the 'strong' is the bound merchant's son, which makes strength a matter of worth rather than of office.

gains.a: the women's curse is seen to rest on a received rule about provoking the stronger, not on mere anger
gains.b: the couplet is shown to be usable against a king, with the strong one being the person he has in chains

links.note: The Kural says the many lack because few do penance; the city women say they lose Civakan because they did no penance.
links.teaches: The couplet's account of why most people lack is turned into a mourner's self-blame, so lack of penance explains not poverty but the loss of a beloved, and the women accuse themselves while blaming the king and the father in the same verse.

gains.a: the lament's first cry is seen to rest on the ethical rule that what one keeps is earned by austerity
gains.b: the couplet's severe claim is shown working as consolation and self-reproach in grief, a use its general form does not show

links.note: Saccandan, ringed in his palace, was a roaring lion hemmed in at a cave mouth and died fighting; his son, seized by the same usurper, goes as a lion bound with a spider's thread.
links.teaches: The lion image marks the difference between father and son: the father was caught by force and fought to death, the son could break his bond at will and keeps it, so the son survives the trap the father did not.

links.note: The patikam tells that the god Civakan once helped untied the flower-cord with which soldiers had bound his arms.
links.teaches: The bond that holds the lion here is as weak as a spider's thread and is in fact loosed by a god, so the image of 1116 is fulfilled literally: it is never the king's force that holds him.

links.note: Civakan let himself be bound because his parents asked it and told him his manhood would not be lessened; here he goes bound like a lion held by a spider's thread.
links.teaches: The thread that binds the lion is the parents' word of 1091, so the spider's thread is the image of consent, and the arrest becomes a test of filial obedience rather than of strength.

links.note: The Kural tells those who serve hot-tempered kings to be like those warming at a fire, neither too far nor too near; Kantukkatan judges the king's anger a fire that burns all who come near and sends gold to quench it.
links.teaches: The Kural's fire teaches distance, while the merchant adds a remedy, gold poured like rain, so the pair shows a courtier's caution and a merchant's purchase as two answers to the same burning king.

gains.a: Kantukkatan's payment is seen as a known prudence toward royal anger, not mere fear
gains.b: the couplet's image is shown to allow a means of putting the fire out, which its advice of keeping distance leaves aside

links.note: Kantukkatan reasoned that opposing a king is the work of the doomed and that sending his son bound would cool the king's anger; now he adds twelve crores of gold to quench it.
links.teaches: The father's policy of submission is completed by payment, so between these two verses his defiant words to the crowd (1114-1115) stand as consolation only, and his actual answer to the king is obedience bought with gold.

source_issues: 1096, 1098, 1108, 1109, 1113-1117 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build; the joins look sound.
1106 line 1 (மாதரார்கள் கற்பினுக்கு உடைந்த) and 1110 line 3 (பாக்கயம், perhaps for பாக்கியம்) are hard to construe as written.
1114 line 2 (வேறிரு கூறு செய்வான் றுன்னினான்) runs words across the join and the first person of 1114-1115 makes the speaker uncertain.
